docs.title: Environments
docs.description: An environment owns the scene, robots, observations, and restorable world state. Tasks can reuse one environment with different tools, instructions, and success criteria.

docs.title: Errors and Recovery
docs.description: Error injection lets a task expose an agent to temporary execution failures or altered perception. Distinguish an error being available, selected for a stage, and actually triggered on a tool call.

docs.title: Execution and Concurrency
docs.description: Three kinds of parallelism are independent: multiple robots in one scene, multiple simulated environments, and multiple models inside an agent system.

docs.title: Concepts and Architecture
docs.description: MAGMA separates the interaction an agent must solve from the capabilities used to execute it. A scenario packages reusable components; a task assembles an interaction; stages define how progress is checked.

docs.title: Perfect Traces
docs.description: A PerfectTrace is a declared reference interaction: user messages, tool calls, expected results, and agent messages. It is not a recorded physics trajectory or proof that a simulated task can be completed.

docs.title: Requests and Constraints
docs.description: A request describes one possible interaction event during task construction: an action request, a rule update, a question, or an interruption. It can produce several stages.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.description: A scenario is a reusable application domain: its environments, task constructors, action capabilities, and optional skills. A Python distribution can provide one or several scenarios.

docs.title: Stages and Interaction
docs.description: A stage declares the next checkpoint of an interaction. Tools describe available actions; goals and stage verification determine whether those actions accomplished the objective.

docs.title: State and Observations
docs.description: Use the state owned by the layer you are changing.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.description: A task is one runnable interaction. It connects an environment, a tools API, an initial situation, and an ordered list of stages.

docs.title: Tools and Skills
docs.description: A tool is an elementary capability offered by the scenario. A skill orchestrates tools over time, retaining its own per-call state.

docs.title: Create an Environment
docs.description: Create environments in your provider package when an installed environment no longer fits your scenario. The first task can reuse an existing environment; environment authoring is a separate step.

docs.title: Create a Stage
docs.description: The first package tutorial defines a complete PressNamedButton stage. Reuse that pattern for a first action checkpoint.

docs.title: Create a Tool
docs.description: This example adds a detection tool to your button scenario. It reuses the physical button implementation while explicitly exposing both methods in your concrete API.

docs.title: Verify Execution Logs
docs.description: Use logs when the way an action was performed matters, such as pressing buttons in order or registering a particular attribute. Environment goals answer whether the world is correct; logs preserve execution evidence.

docs.title: Make Stages Reusable
docs.description: A reusable stage keeps the same verification logic while accepting different objectives and interaction inputs. Parameterize the expected arrangement and checkpoint instead of writing a new class for each task.

docs.title: Use Articulated Objects
docs.description: An articulated object exposes more than a rigid actor pose: tools and goals may need joint positions, limits, and machine state. Define that observation contract in your own environment module.

docs.title: Compose Tools into a Skill
docs.description: Use a skill when one action should orchestrate several tool calls, inspect intermediate results, and retain progress. The current API replaces the old ToolExecution(..., redo=...) pattern with explicit skill execution.

docs.title: Change and Preserve Environment State
docs.description: Choose the mechanism matching the cause of the change.

docs.title: Inject a Temporary Tool Failure
docs.description: Begin with one temporary execution error before adding perception or accessibility changes.

docs.title: Coordinate Robots and Shared Resources
docs.description: First make each tool work on one robot. Then specify robot identity and how simultaneous calls share resources.

docs.title: Create Your Own Scenario Package
docs.description: This tutorial creates my_buttons.FirstTask in your own package. It reuses an installed environment and tools, and supplies a custom task and stage. At the end, the scenario is discoverable and its button tool can be exercised interactively.

docs.title: Create a Task Preset
docs.description: Start from FirstTask in your own package. A preset assembles existing components into an explicit interaction.

docs.title: Test Your Scenario
docs.description: If you followed the first tutorial, you have a preset: a task whose stages are already assembled. Follow Check discovery and Test tools in simulation below. That is enough to check the physical button example.

docs.title: Ask the Agent a Question
docs.description: Use a text-only stage when success depends on the agent answering a question.

docs.title: Introduce Persistent Rules
docs.description: A persistent rule has a construction-side effect and an interaction-side presentation. Keep those two parts consistent.

docs.title: Interrupt and Resume an Interaction
docs.description: Use an interruption when a direct instruction must be handled while a previous action sequence has not yet reached its completion answer.

docs.title: Require Clarification from the Agent
docs.description: A clarification stage checks whether the agent asks for information it does not have. It is a text-only objective, not a tool that fills in missing data silently.

docs.title: Modify Task Attributes
docs.description: Use attribute edits when the agent must add or remove a known value, such as a newly announced delivery location. This changes task vocabulary, not the physical scene.

docs.title: Build a Multi-stage Interaction
docs.description: One user instruction can require several independently verified actions. Keep the first instruction explicit and subsequent continuation inputs empty.

docs.title: Create Scenarios and Tasks
docs.description: Build a first task in your own package, then add only the components and interactions you need.

docs.title: Build Tasks with Requests
docs.description: Once a preset works, use a TaskDefinition to construct varied interactions. This example extends your package and reuses PressNamedButton.

docs.title: Randomize Public Vocabulary
docs.description: Vocabulary randomization changes names and descriptions exposed to the model while keeping runtime identifiers stable. It is distinct from physical scene randomization and request sampling.

docs.title: Add an Optional Perfect Trace
docs.description: Add a perfect trace only when a consuming workflow needs a declared reference interaction. Ordinary request construction can leave buildperfecttrace unimplemented, returning None through BaseRequest.

docs.title: Make Components Reconstructible
docs.description: Some consumers save task initialization and stage specifications for replay or artifact generation. Execution and serialization are distinct capabilities.

docs.title: Stage Contract
docs.description: Import stage classes and parameter dataclasses from magmacore.simulation.stage; import StageInput and instructions from magmacore.simulation.data_structures.

docs.title: Task Preset Contract
docs.description: Import BaseTask, InitializationParameters, and TaskMetadata from magma_core.simulation.tasks.

docs.title: Task Definitions and Requests
docs.description: Import TaskDefinition from magmacore.simulation.tasks, BaseRequest from magmacore.simulation.requests, and TaskState / RuleRenderer from magma_core.simulation.state.

docs.title: Tool Execution and Result Contract
docs.description: Import BaseToolsAPI and registertool from magmacore.simulation.tools. Execution data structures are exported from magmacore.simulation.datastructures.

docs.title: Error Injection Contract
docs.description: BaseError is exported by magmacore.simulation.errors. Declare compatible classes in @registertool(errors=...), optionally wrapped in ToolErrorSupport(error_type, pre=True, post=True).

docs.title: Perfect Trace Contract
docs.description: Core trace events live in magmacore.domain.perfecttrace and are also re-exported from magma_core.simulation.requests.

docs.title: Scenario Providers
docs.description: Import ScenarioManifest from magma_scenarios.manifest.

docs.title: Skill Contract
docs.description: Import BaseSkill, SkillSpec, SkillTick, CallTick, and MessTick from magma_core.simulation.skills.

docs.title: Constraint Building Blocks
docs.description: Core classes live in magma_core.simulation.constraints:

docs.title: Error Templates
docs.description: The installed magma_scenarios.templates.errors exports:

docs.title: Goal Predicates
docs.description: Import predicates from magma_core.simulation.goals.

docs.title: Request Building Blocks
docs.description: BaseRequest[ParametersT] lives in magma_core.simulation.requests. Concrete requests must sample parameters and create stages.

docs.title: Stage Templates
docs.description: Core templates are exported from magma_core.simulation.stage.
